Title: Birds of Nebraska
Content: The state of Nebraska is a bird lover's paradise. All `text(year)` long, birds of all colors and sizes fly to and from the state. Around `460` species of birds can be spotted in Nebraska. In fact, birds are so beloved that festivals have even sprung up around some of these feathered celebrities.

Springtime in Nebraska brings with it a beautiful sight. Over a `text(quarter)` of a `text(million)` sandhill cranes begin to gather. They are getting ready for their migration north for the summer. These tall birds are known for their long legs. They stroll through water and over land in search of plants, rodents, bugs, and even snakes for food. Their loud trumpeting calls echo across the Platte River. The sky and ground are filled with their cream-colored feathers. These beautiful creatures help attract `text(thousands)` of visitors to Nebraska `text(year)` after `text(year)`.

Another remarkable gathering of birds occurs at the Harlan County Reservoir, where `text(thousands)` of white pelicans soar majestically across the water and through the sky. Groups of up to `100` of these huge birds travel together. They steadily spiral upward using air currents to help them rise. With a wingspan of up to `text(9.5 feet)`, they can circle for long periods of time with little effort. The only North American bird with a greater wingspan than the pelican is the California condor. When it is time for a snack, the pelican floats on the water, scooping fish in its long beak. Pelicans often hunt together in shallow water, cooperating to direct fish toward one another. They eat around `text(four pounds)` of fish a `text(day)`, so this kind of cooperation is beneficial for them.

Long ago, cowboys riding across the plains began calling burrowing owls “howdy birds.” The small birds would pop their heads out of burrows in the ground and appear to give passersby a friendly nod as if wishing them well. Burrowing owls are still nodding in Nebraska today, though their numbers have declined. Efforts to reduce prairie dog populations have affected the owls as well. These speckled brown birds grow to a little less than `text(one foot)` tall. They are also known for their strikingly bright yellow eyes, which help them to hunt at night. They mostly eat insects and small mammals. When danger is near, they will call out an alarm to warn other burrowing birds to seek the safety of their homes.

The sandhill crane, the white pelican, and the burrowing owl are only `text(three)` of the fascinating birds that make their homes in Nebraska for at least part of the `text(year)`. It is easy to see why birdwatchers flock to the state to watch and study these birds.
